analysis.one_liner: Requires gun dealers and their staff to get annual training, carry liability insurance, and block suspected straw purchases.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote or any action on the House floor and died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require federally licensed gun dealers, manufacturers, and importers and their employees to pass an annual Attorney General training course on spotting straw purchases, gun trafficking, and buyers at risk of harming themselves or others. It would require dealers to post warning signs, keep written protocols at the counter, secure inventory overnight against theft, and carry at least $1 million in business liability insurance (small dealers selling 20 or fewer guns a year are exempted from the insurance rule). It would make it a crime to knowingly sell to straw purchasers, traffickers, or intoxicated buyers, with penalties including license suspension or revocation.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by gun trafficking and gun violence, since dealers would be required to screen out straw purchasers and traffickers, secure inventory against theft, and carry insurance that can compensate victims of negligent sales. Law-abiding gun buyers are also nominally served, since the bill targets unlawful transfers rather than lawful purchases.

how_it_helps.text: Dealers and employees must complete annual training, including a 20-question exam, on recognizing straw purchasers, traffickers, intoxicated buyers, and people at risk of self-harm before they can legally transfer a firearm.

Dealers are prohibited from knowingly transferring firearms to straw purchasers, gun traffickers, or intoxicated individuals, and must immediately notify ATF and local police of suspected straw purchases or trafficking.
Dealers must keep written protocols at every point of sale describing the indicators of straw purchasing and gun trafficking, and must post a notice describing the signs of unlawful purchases.
Dealers must secure their inventory with locking devices or containers whenever the store is closed, to prevent burglaries that supply the illegal market with stolen guns.

Dealers selling more than 20 guns a year must carry at least $1 million in general business and liability insurance covering negligent or unlawful transfers, and violations can bring fines, up to 18 months in jail, or license suspension or revocation.

analysis.who_pays: Licensed firearms dealers, manufacturers, and importers, who would bear training and certification requirements, insurance premiums, secure-storage equipment costs, and legal exposure for sales to people they had reason to know were acting unlawfully. The Justice Department would also bear the cost of building and maintaining the training course, certification database, and written protocols.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall hardest on small gun shops: annual training for every employee, locking storage for the whole inventory, and counter protocols could be burdensome for a small dealer, though dealers selling 20 or fewer guns a year are exempt from the insurance mandate.

The bill makes it a crime to sell to someone the dealer 'knows or has reasonable cause to know' is a straw purchaser, trafficker, intoxicated, or about to harm someone — a standard gun-rights critics argue is vague enough to expose dealers for refusing few sales or chill lawful ones, and which became a core objection from the industry and gun-rights groups to dealer-conduct rules of this kind.

The requirement that employees pass a background check and hold a renewable certificate before transferring a firearm adds a government credential to every retail transaction, which opponents framed as an added barrier to legal gun ownership.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core rules — training to spot straw buyers, locking up inventory overnight, and refusing obvious traffickers — are modest, targeted steps aimed at the supply side of illegal guns rather than at lawful buyers, and the bill exempts the smallest sellers from its costliest requirement. The strongest honest objection is the vagueness of the 'reasonable cause to know' standard and the added cost and credentialing burden on small dealers; whether those costs are worth the expected reduction in trafficked guns is a judgment the record does not settle, because the bill never received a hearing or vote where it could be tested or amended.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, moved to its Crime subcommittee a year later, and died when the Congress ended without ever getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Jason Crow introduced the bill on October 22, 2021, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On November 1, 2022, about a year after introduction, it was referred to the subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security — the last action of any kind in the bill's history.
No hearing, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Licensed firearms dealers, manufacturers, and importers are better off, because none of the training, insurance, secure-storage, and liability rules ever took effect; the FBI and ATF's role in the illegal gun market was left unchanged.

for.name: Rep. Jason Crow
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and lined up 27 original cosponsors from his own party.

for.name: 27 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every listed supporter was a Democrat, and none was a Republican.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Jerrold Nadler, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill during the 15 months it had jurisdiction; the furthest it moved was referral to the Crime subcommittee in November 2022, a year after introduction.

sides.party_line_note: All 28 supporters — the sponsor and 27 cosponsors — were House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsor and no recorded opposition votes because the bill never reached one.

industries.note: Dealers would bear annual employee training and certification, mandatory $1 million liability insurance for higher-volume sellers, locked overnight storage, and criminal and civil exposure for sales to suspected straw buyers or traffickers. Some dealers argue the rules penalize lawful businesses for criminals' actions; supporters argue a small share of irresponsible dealers supply much of the illegal market.
The bill applies the same training, certification, and conduct rules to licensed manufacturers and importers, adding compliance costs. The bulk of the burden still falls on the retail side.
Higher-volume dealers would be required to buy at least $1 million in general business and liability coverage, creating a new market of mandated customers for insurers licensed in each state.
